I think we have. A lot of software uses FAR too much memory/storage/CPU than it should for what it does. With super powerful computers, programmers have become too lazy to optimize

It's not always our fault. Programmers get paid by their employer. Managers rarely want to hear about optimisation and will rush software out of the door as quickly as they can. I've written stuff that was horrible and slow but I had a deadline that I had to meet or risk my job, no time allowed for doing the job properly when I could be moved onto another project so that my employer gets their moneys-worth from employing me.

The technical expertise of one type has been traded for the technical expertise of different types. Modern game developers have to deal with a variety of hardware. True, there are a few unified interfaces, but doing something in, say, OpenGL is half "OpenGL" and half "which extension flags are supported on this device?" Multiple CPUs, DMA, multiple peripherals, multiple resolutions, not being allowed control over the hardware right at the metal, online play, all these things add a lot of complexity in ways that aren't so easy to explain -- or cool enough to appreciate -- in a 10 minute video. It's no wonder so many games are built on top of 3rd party engines and frameworks.

As a result, in the old days, the same game on a different platforms could be radically different. Your platform might get the superior version of Cybernoid and the inferior version of Marble Madness. There might be a "best" version of any given game these days, but the differences between them isn't nearly as big as it used to be.

Edit: There are people still doing things oldschool, there is still a very lively NES homebrew scene to name one!
